questions.prompt: Complete: "By the time the guests arrived, Yasmine ___ all the food."
questions.explanation: "By the time" signals that one past action was completed before another past event. The past perfect (had prepared) is required: Yasmine finished the food first, then the guests arrived. Past simple (prepared) ignores the sequence; past continuous (was preparing) implies it was unfinished; present perfect (has prepared) is impossible in a past context.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains a grammatical error?

options.text: He used to walk to school every day.
She used to be afraid of spiders.
They used to played football on Fridays.
We used to live near the sea.

questions.explanation: "Used to" is always followed by the base form (infinitive without to is already included in the structure: used to + base verb). "Played" is a past form — writing "used to played" double-marks the past. The correct form is "used to play". "He used to walk to school every day", "She used to be afraid of spiders" and "We used to live near the sea" all correctly use "used to" + base verb.

questions.prompt: Complete: "When I ___ to the station, the train already ___ ."
questions.explanation: Two past events in sequence: arriving at the station (past simple: got) is the reference point; the train leaving happened before that (past perfect: had left). "Already" reinforces the earlier completion. "had got / left" reverses the logic — the arrival cannot precede itself with past perfect here. "was getting / left" is wrong because "getting" implies the journey was still in progress when the train left. "got / has left" mixes past simple with present perfect, which is grammatically impossible.

questions.prompt: Complete: "He ___ the report three times before he ___ it to his teacher."
questions.explanation: The checking happened before the submitting — both are past events, but checking is the earlier one. The past perfect (had checked) marks it as prior; the past simple (submitted) marks the later reference event. "checked / submitted"(both past simple) is grammatically possible in informal speech but loses the precise sequence signal required at exam level. "was checking / had submitted" wrongly uses past perfect for the later action. "has checked / submitted" wrongly uses present perfect in a fully past context.

options.text: While the phone rang, I was cooking dinner.
When I was having a bath, the doorbell rang.
While I arrived, she was leaving the room.
When she was writing, she was finishing the letter.

questions.explanation: "When I was having a bath, the doorbell rang" is correct: "was having" (past continuous) provides the ongoing background; "rang" (past simple) is the short interrupting event — the classic when-pattern. "While the phone rang, I was cooking dinner" is wrong because "rang" is a short punctual verb and cannot be the background of a "while" clause; it should be "when the phone rang, I was cooking". "While I arrived, she was leaving the room" is wrong because "arrive" is punctual and cannot be a "while" background. "When she was writing, she was finishing the letter" is wrong because "finish" describes a completed result and cannot be past continuous alongside another continuous action.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The police discovered that the thief ___ through the back window and ___ the safe before anyone ___ the alarm."
questions.explanation: The thief's actions (climbing in, emptying the safe) both occurred before the alarm was raised — the reference past event. Past perfect (had climbed, had emptied) correctly places these two earlier actions; past simple (raised) marks the later reference point. "climbed / emptied / raised" loses the sequence entirely. "was climbing / emptied / had raised" wrongly puts "had raised" on the alarm, reversing the logic — the alarm came last, not first. "had climbed / was emptying / raised" uses past continuous for "emptying", implying it was still in progress when the alarm went off, which contradicts the "before" clause.
